items.title: Your mitochondria used to be a separate organism
items.claim: Mitochondria have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide independently of the cell. About 2 billion years ago, a free-living alpha-proteobacterium got engulfed by another cell and stayed.
items.prompt: What's the strongest evidence mitochondria were once independent?

options.text: They are smaller than the host cell

Mitochondrial DNA is circular (like a bacterial chromosome), their ribosomes resemble bacterial ribosomes (and are inhibited by antibiotics like chloramphenicol), and their inner membrane has bacteria-like lipid composition

items.reveal_title: Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiotic theory
items.reveal:
Lynn Margulis proposed in 1967 that mitochondria descend from free-living alpha-proteobacteria, and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria. Her paper was rejected fifteen times before being accepted. The orthodoxy disliked the idea of major evolution happening by merger rather than gradual modification.

The evidence accumulated:
- Circular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
- Bacterial-style ribosomes; sensitive to bacterial antibiotics.
- Double membranes (the outer from the host cell, the inner from the bacterium).
- Replication by binary fission, independent of cell division.
- Phylogenetic analysis: mitochondrial genes group with Rickettsia (intracellular alpha-proteobacteria).

All eukaryotes (including animals, plants, fungi) descend from this single ancient merger. Without it, complex life wouldn't exist.
items.why: Evolution is taught as branching divergence. Some of the most important steps came from merger — two organisms becoming one.

items.title: Stomata are tiny mouths that decide between starving and drying
items.claim: A leaf has hundreds of stomata per square millimetre. Open them: CO2 enters for photosynthesis but water evaporates away. Close them: water is saved but photosynthesis stalls. Plants must decide minute by minute.
items.prompt: How do guard cells open and close the stomatal pore?

options.text: Guard cells actively pump K+ ions in; water follows by osmosis; the cell swells; thicker inner walls force the cell to bow outward, opening the pore. Reverse the process to close

items.reveal:
Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells. Their inner walls (facing the pore) are thicker and less elastic than their outer walls.

Opening: blue light activates a proton pump (H+-ATPase). The cells become more negative inside; K+ flows in via channels. Cl- and malate follow. Water enters by osmosis. Turgor rises. The thinner outer walls expand more than the inner walls, pulling the cells apart and opening the pore.

Closing: ABA (abscisic acid, the drought-stress hormone) triggers K+ efflux. The cells lose water and shrink. The pore closes.

Most plants close stomata at night (no photosynthesis needed) and during drought. CAM plants invert this. Wheat loses ~500 kg of water per kg of grain produced — most through stomata.

Climate change is forcing plants to evolve stomatal density: rising CO2 lets leaves get the same carbon with fewer stomata, reducing water loss.
items.why: Stomatal regulation is the central trade-off of land plant life. Engineering stomata for higher water-use efficiency is a major target of crop science.

items.title: You convert nitrogen waste into your own pee chemistry every day
items.claim: Breaking down amino acids releases ammonia (NH3) — toxic to cells at concentrations above ~50 micromolar. Mammals convert it to urea, a relatively harmless molecule that can be safely concentrated and excreted in urine. Fish dump ammonia directly into water; birds convert it to uric acid.
items.prompt: Why do different animals handle nitrogen waste differently?

options.text: Water availability drives the choice: fish (ammoniotelic, ammonia) need lots of water for dilution; mammals (ureotelic, urea) use moderate water; birds and reptiles (uricotelic, uric acid) save water by making a near-solid waste — important for desert and egg-laying animals

items.reveal:
Ammonia (NH3): produced by deamination of amino acids. Toxic at low concentrations. Fish, most aquatic invertebrates excrete it directly through gills — the surrounding water dilutes it.

Urea: synthesised by the urea cycle in the liver (Krebs and Henseleit, 1932 — the same Hans Krebs who later won the Nobel for the citric acid cycle). Five reactions, costs 4 ATP per urea. Each urea carries 2 nitrogen atoms. Soluble, moderately concentrated in urine (up to ~50x blood concentration in humans).

Uric acid: birds, reptiles, insects. Synthesis costs even more energy than urea (~10 ATP per nitrogen handled) but precipitates as semi-solid pellets, requiring almost no water for excretion. The white component of bird droppings is uric acid.

Note: egg-laying animals (birds, reptiles, monotremes) need a non-toxic, water-poor waste form that won't poison the developing embryo. Uric acid fits the niche.

In humans, uric acid is a byproduct of nucleic acid breakdown (not protein). Gout is precipitation of uric acid crystals in joints.

Marine mammals (whales, seals) face the opposite challenge: no fresh water for dilution. They use highly concentrated urine instead.
items.why: Waste seems like a non-design decision. The form of nitrogen excretion is one of evolution's deepest trade-offs — tying physiology, water economy and even reproductive biology together.
